instructional_purpose: Pushes the diminutive template family past the simple three-consonant base into four-consonant stems, stems carrying a prefixed letter or a feminine ending, stems whose weak radical is invisible in the citation form, and two-element proper names. Pairs that formal machinery with the four pragmatic values (small size, affection, belittlement, nearness in time) that decide why a speaker reaches for the form at all.
concepts_taught: diminution as a template overlay imposed on an existing noun rather than a fresh derivation from the root
two base templates for three-consonant stems, selected by whether the base carries a long medial vowel
a distinct four-slot template for four-consonant stems
retention of a feminine ending under diminution
diminution of a two-element proper name affects only the first element
restoration of a weak final radical that the base form suppresses
treatment of a stem-initial prefixed mim: the prefix stays and the remainder is re-templated
deletion of a connecting hamza in stems that begin with one
four semantic values of the diminutive and their dependence on speaker stance
diminutive template versus lookalike adjectival and participial templates

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Every diminutive shares a fixed vowel skeleton: damma on the first stem consonant, fatha on the second, and an inserted glide immediately after the second.
Choice between the two three-consonant diminutive templates is decided by the presence of a long vowel or a geminate in the middle of the base.
Four-consonant stems take a template with a fourth slot and kasra on the third consonant.
The lesson's own inventory contains a base with a long vowel in the fourth slot whose diminutive keeps that long vowel, which the stated four-consonant rule does not generate.
A feminine ending on the base is preserved unchanged in the diminutive.
In a two-element name only the first element is diminutized; the second is untouched.
A three-consonant noun with a suppressed weak final radical restores that radical and additionally acquires a feminine ending in the diminutive.

The added feminine ending in such forms is presented as a consequence of restoring the weak radical, whereas the traditional account ties it to the base noun's covert feminine gender; the lesson conflates two independent rules.
A proper name with no written feminine ending is said to retain an implicit feminine marker under diminution.
Stems opening with a connecting hamza lose it and the remaining consonants take the ordinary diminutive skeleton.
The same diminutive form can carry affection or contempt; only speaker stance and situation separate them.
Adverbial bases of time yield diminutives meaning shortly before or shortly after the reference point.

recognition_criteria: a noun whose first consonant carries damma and whose second carries fatha, with a glide directly after the second
a glide in the stem that has no counterpart in the lexeme's root
a base lexeme recoverable by stripping the inserted glide and restoring the base vowels
a feminine ending or a prefixed letter that survives unchanged from the base

the four-slot template applies only to four-consonant stems

instructional_purpose: Adds four low-frequency broken-plural templates to the learner's inventory and, more importantly, teaches that the choice among them is licensed by properties of the singular: its template, whether its final radical is geminate or weak, whether its referent is human, and whether the quality it names is inherent or an afflicted condition. Ties the survival of these plurals to technical, legal, devotional, and belletristic registers.
concepts_taught: broken pluralisation as template replacement rather than affixation
a template for human-referring adjectives of the فَعيل shape naming inherent qualities
a prefixed template for فَعيل stems whose final radical is geminate or weak
gemination collapse when the plural brings two identical radicals together
an archaic lexically-restricted template surviving in trade and collective vocabulary
a template clustering around involuntary or afflicted states
semantics as a licensing condition, not merely a correlation
register distribution: which text types preserve which rare plurals
non-predictability and the resulting need for lexical lookup

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Human-referring adjectives of the فَعيل shape denoting inherent qualities take the فُعَلاء plural.
فَعيل stems with a geminate or weak final radical take the prefixed أَفعِلاء plural instead.
When the plural template brings two identical radicals into contact they collapse into a geminate, so the written form must carry the gemination.
An active-participle stem naming a scholarly capacity is admitted into the فُعَلاء class as a stated exception because its referent is human and its quality inherent.
The فِعْلان template is lexically restricted and cannot be extended to new stems.
The فُعالى class groups referents in involuntary or afflicted states, and this semantic clustering is presented as motivated rather than accidental.
The lesson files several stems ending in a shortened alif under the same فُعالى heading as stems ending in a long alif-hamza sequence, treating two distinct output shapes as one class.
A feminine-ended singular naming a human office is pluralised by the human-quality template despite its feminine ending.
None of the four templates is fully predictable from the singular; a dictionary check is the final authority.
One inventory item in the trade-register list is presented through a template name used as if it were an ordinary lexeme.
Rare plurals survive disproportionately in medical, legal, devotional, court-administrative and belletristic registers rather than in ordinary speech.
The rhymed-prose showpiece attributed to a named classical author is presented as an illustration of virtuosic plural stacking; the attribution is asserted, not evidenced in the lesson.

recognition_criteria: a plural ending in a long vowel plus hamza with damma-fatha vowelling on the stem, pointing to the human-quality class
the same long ending but with a prefixed hamza and kasra inside, pointing to the geminate or weak-final class
gemination inside a prefixed plural signalling an underlying doubled radical in the singular
a plural in a long vowel plus nun with no sound-plural agreement behaviour, pointing to the archaic collective class
a plural ending in a shortened alif with an affliction reading
singular referent humanity as the first filter on which class is even available
procedures: check whether the singular referent is human and rational
check the singular template and whether it names an inherent quality
inspect the final radical for gemination or weakness
check whether the meaning is an involuntary or afflicted condition
if none of the filters resolves the case, treat the plural as lexical and look it up
when the geminate class applies, apply gemination collapse in the written output
conditions: human and rational reference for the inherent-quality class
geminate or weak final radical for the prefixed class
affliction or temporary condition semantics for the shortened-alif class
prior lexical attestation for the archaic collective class
exceptions: an active-participle singular admitted into a class otherwise defined over a different singular template
a feminine-ended singular taking a masculine human-quality plural
the archaic collective class refusing extension even where the semantics would fit
contrasts: inherent quality versus afflicted state as the divider between two templates of similar length
geminate final radical versus sound final radical inside the same prefixed class
human-referring versus non-human singulars, the latter barred from the quality class
rare register-bound plurals versus the everyday plural of the same lexeme
productive templates versus lexically frozen ones

common_mistakes.pattern: extending the human-quality plural template to a non-human noun
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the template is licensed by rational reference; without it the output is not a possible plural of that stem
common_mistakes.correction_principle: test referent humanity before template selection

common_mistakes.pattern: omitting the prefixed hamza in the geminate or weak-final class
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the prefix is part of the template, not an optional embellishment, and its absence produces a non-word
common_mistakes.correction_principle: the template is a whole shape including its prefix

common_mistakes.pattern: confusing the inherent-quality class with the affliction class

common_mistakes.correction_principle: let the semantic type of the singular decide, not surface similarity of the two plurals

common_mistakes.pattern: treating the archaic collective template as productive

common_mistakes.correction_principle: restricted templates are licensed item by item, never by analogy

common_mistakes.pattern: writing a prefixed plural of a geminate-final singular without the gemination
common_mistakes.why_wrong: the two identical radicals brought together must surface as a single geminated consonant
common_mistakes.correction_principle: apply the contact rule after template imposition, then write the result

proposed_new_units.summary: A licensing table mapping singular properties (template, referent humanity, final-radical class, inherent-quality versus afflicted-state semantics, lexical restriction) to the admissible rare plural templates, with an explicit lexical-fallback verdict when no condition resolves.

instructional_purpose: Introduces second-order pluralisation, where an existing broken plural is itself pluralised, and insists that the second layer is not a quantity increase but a shift to groupings, categories, or kinds. Locates the phenomenon in catalogue-like technical, administrative, and elevated literary writing and warns that it cannot be generated at will.
concepts_taught: a plural form serving as the input to a further pluralisation
the semantic shift from plurality of items to plurality of groupings or categories
the dominant second-layer strategy: a sound feminine ending attached to an existing broken plural
a rarer second-layer strategy: one broken template replacing another
lexical restriction: the phenomenon is item-by-item, not rule-driven
idiomatic drift of some second-layer forms into social or abstract senses
register distribution across catalogues, registers of notables, elevated verse, and scriptural or legal citation
the historical claim that an early grammarian first classified the phenomenon

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A broken plural can itself take a further plural form.
The second layer contributes a collection or category reading rather than a larger count.
The most common second-layer strategy is suffixation of the sound feminine plural ending to the broken plural.
A minority of items pluralise a broken plural with another broken template.
The phenomenon is lexically restricted and cannot be freely extended to arbitrary plurals.
Certain second-layer forms have drifted to social-group senses such as leading families or notables that are no longer compositional.
A medical use of one second-layer form as a technical term for a co-occurring symptom cluster is presented as established terminology.
One row of the summary table offers a doubly-suffixed heavenly-bodies form which the lesson itself brackets as rare or archaic, so it is offered and withdrawn in the same line.
The classification of second-order plurals is credited to a named early grammarian, with a quotation and a table presented as excerpted from his book.
Case behaviour of second-layer forms is ordinary and unaffected by the extra layer.
In everyday usage the first plural suffices and the second layer is confined to formal writing.

proposed_new_units.summary: Discriminates a second-order plural built on a broken plural from a first plural built on the singular and from an unrelated broken plural of the same singular, and records the closed list of licensed items together with the grouping-or-category reading the extra layer contributes.
proposed_new_units.why_existing_insufficient: u-s08 treats number as a single alternation between singular, dual, and plural; it has no representation for a plural serving as a derivational base, no closed-list licensing, and no semantic operator attached to a second layer.

instructional_purpose: Presents two verbal-noun strategies that dominate technical and formal writing: the mim-initial verbal noun, whose Form I shape is set by the present-stem vowel and whose derived-form shape coincides with the passive participle, and the suffix-built abstract noun that turns a noun or adjective into a quality term. Trains the learner to feel the concreteness contrast between a mim-initial form and the ordinary verbal noun of the same root.
concepts_taught: a verbal noun formed with a prefixed mim alongside the ordinary verbal noun of the same root
Form I template selection driven by the vowel of the middle radical in the present stem
a variant with a feminine ending for certain cognitive and abstract senses
derived-form mim verbal nouns coinciding in shape with the passive participle
systematic homography with place and time nouns built on the same templates
the suffix-built abstract noun and its restriction to nominal and adjectival bases
obligatory feminine ending on the suffix-built abstract noun
process versus result-or-source as the semantic split between the two verbal-noun types
register profile: technical, scholarly, administrative, and honorific usage

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The mim-initial verbal noun names the action like an ordinary verbal noun but leans toward its source, occasion, or concrete instance.
For Form I, kasra on the middle radical of the present stem yields the kasra-vowelled mim template, while fatha or damma yields the fatha-vowelled one.
The mim-initial verbal noun and the place-or-time noun share the same templates, so only context separates the two functions.
For Forms II to X the mim verbal noun is identical in shape to the passive participle.

The lesson heads one table with the fatha-vowelled feminine template while listing under it items it elsewhere assigns to the kasra-vowelled template, and it says so in a note; the table and the note disagree.
Some items in that feminine-ended list are presented as mim verbal nouns although they are more usually treated as nouns of quality or of scene.
Adding the abstract-noun suffix to a noun or adjective produces an abstract quality term.
The abstract-noun suffix attaches to nominal and adjectival bases but not to verbs.
The suffix-built abstract noun is always feminine and cannot drop the ending.
Where a root has both an ordinary and a mim-initial verbal noun, the former reads as process and the latter as result, source, or specific instance.
The mystical versus practical contrast drawn between one pair of knowledge nouns is a lexical-semantic claim about two particular items, not a general consequence of the templates.
Both formations are diagnostic of technical, scholarly, administrative, and honorific registers.

process semantics versus result or source semantics

common_mistakes.correction_principle: the function is decided by the syntactic and semantic context, never by the shape alone

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The fatha-initial Form I template names one occurrence of the action.
The kasra-initial Form I template names the manner in which the action is performed.
The only formal difference between the two is the vowel on the first radical.
Because that vowel is not written in unvocalised text, the two are indistinguishable in an ordinary running orthography.
For derived forms whose verbal noun already ends in the feminine marker, single-occurrence sense is expressed by adding the word for 'one'.

The lesson states that rule as general for derived forms, yet its own Form VIII illustration is a verbal noun that has taken the feminine ending directly, which is the traditional derived-form procedure; the stated rule and the example do not match.
The manner template is essentially confined to Form I; derived forms use descriptive paraphrase instead.
The manner template is less productive than the occurrence template, and many roots lack one member of the pair.
A hollow root's manner noun surfaces with a long vowel produced by the weak radical, which the lesson lists without deriving.
One occurrence noun is spelled identically to a grammatical vowel-name and is separated only by context.
Isolating an action as a single occurrence is a stylistic device that gives narrative weight to a moment.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: A generic collective denotes a species or mass and is morphologically singular while referring to many.
Adding the feminine marker to a generic collective extracts one individual of that species.
The unit noun is derived from the collective; the collective is not a plural of the unit.
The unit noun pluralises with the sound feminine ending for small counts.
A separate class of collectives has no unit counterpart formed by the feminine marker.
Collectives admit either feminine singular or masculine plural agreement.

The lesson's agreement table pairs a masculine collective head with a feminine singular predicate and separately offers a masculine plural predicate labelled rare or dialectal; both rows need checking before either is projected onto text.

One listed unit-less collective is a suppletive-looking plural of a human noun, whose classification as a collective rather than a broken plural is a traditional analytical decision.
Nouns that merely have broken plurals are not collectives, even when their referents come in quantity.
The functional contrast between mass generosity and countable accounting is illustrated through a classical anecdote attributed to a named author.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: Registers are distinguished by co-occurring bundles of features rather than by any single marker.
The administrative variety is characterised by passive voice, chains of verbal nouns in annexation, and frozen formulas.
The narrative variety is characterised by past-tense dominance and a small set of sequential and temporal connectors.
The oratorical variety is characterised by rhymed prose and syntactic parallelism.
Rhymed prose is prose: it rhymes at phrase ends but is not built on a poetic metre.

The lesson lists the everyday spoken variety among the registers said to exist inside the literary standard, which contradicts its own opening definition of the two as historically distinct varieties.
Legal language avoids metaphor because ambiguity in law risks injustice, a position attributed to a named historian.
There is no single correct variety; correctness is indexed to situation.
The illustrative sermon, chronicle extract, and official notice are lesson-composed specimens presented as representative of their registers.
Classical works shift register internally, so a single-register reading of a whole work misses authorial intent.
The register spectrum can be linearly ordered from informal to formal.

instructional_purpose: Takes the most formal register isolated in the previous lesson and dissects its three structural pillars: agent-suppressing passives, inherited formulaic phrases, and long chains of verbal nouns in annexation that replace finite clauses. Explains deliberate redundancy as a precision device and uses a forgery anecdote to show that the register is imitable but that emotional excess betrays the imitation.

linguistic_propositions.proposition: The passive is preferred in legal writing because suppressing the agent makes the ruling appear to issue from the law itself.
Augmented verb forms opening with a connecting hamza take a distinctive passive vowelling that is a formal marker of the register.
Frozen formulas are inherited unchanged because courts have already settled their interpretation.
Legal prose replaces finite clauses with chains of verbal nouns in annexation, every non-initial member of which is genitive.
Verbal nouns are preferred because they carry no tense, mood, or aspect and therefore introduce no temporal ambiguity.
Pairing two near-synonymous passive verbs is precision rather than redundancy, because each covers a different legal ground.
Legal technical terms are not freely substitutable even when their everyday senses overlap.
The register can be imitated by reproducing its passives, formulas, and nominal chains; what exposes the imitation is affective excess rather than any structural error.
A written legal register arose in the second Islamic century out of the need to codify what had been transmitted orally.
A named historian's judgement placing legal language nearer to chancery prose than to poetry is quoted twice across this module.
The two long documentary specimens and the chancery anecdote are lesson-composed or lesson-adapted rather than transcribed sources, though both carry source attributions.
Ambiguity in a legal text is treated as equivalent to potential injustice, which is the stated justification for the whole style.

proposed_new_units.summary: Classifies the passive vowelling of augmented verb forms, in particular those opening with a connecting hamza, so that a passive of an augmented form is not misread as an active or as a different form class.
proposed_new_units.why_existing_insufficient: u-s02 enumerates the derived forms and their active templates; the passive vowelling of the hamza-initial augmented forms is a separate template set that the unit does not carry, and it is the single most reliable formal marker of this register.

proposed_new_units.summary: Holds a closed list of invariant multi-word documentary formulas and marks them as non-compositional units, so that a parser or glosser treats them whole rather than deriving a misleading word-by-word reading.
proposed_new_units.why_existing_insufficient: u-n12 covers cohesion devices as productive grammar; these formulas are lexically frozen items whose interpretation is institutional rather than compositional, which no existing unit is scoped to record.
